days.review: Encoding is how information goes in the first time — the highest-leverage learning skill. Encode well and the forgetting curve flattens; you may keep most of what you learned after a single strong pass. That reduces endless review.

task.do: Pick a topic you studied in the last week. Without re-reading first, rate what % you still have usable grasp of, and list what encoding moves you used originally (reread, map, relate, none). Plan one encoding upgrade for a new section today.
task.capture: Topic; rough retained %; past encoding moves; upgrade plan.

check.q: Given your retained-% estimate and the encoding moves you listed, what does low retention after reread-heavy study imply about encoding versus endless review?
check.rubric: correct: Weak first-pass encoding; review can't fully replace better encoding; cites their data. mostly_correct: Need better encoding vaguely. incorrect: Reread-only flattens forgetting best.
check.exemplar: Low retention after many reread-only hours means the intake process was weak. More review can't fully replace better first-pass encoding. Strong encoding flattens forgetting; weak encoding leaves me relearning.

check.q: Explain your encoding upgrade plan for a new section. Why does it target encoding (how ideas enter) rather than only last-minute retrieval?
check.rubric: correct: Build big-picture structure/connections on the way in. mostly_correct: Study better vaguely. incorrect: Only more cramming; skip organization on entry.
check.exemplar: I'll build a clearer big-picture structure as ideas enter — relate and organize on intake. That's encoding skill, the highest leverage. Last-minute cramming without better entry process keeps the forgetting curve steep.

check.q: Encoding practice can feel slower at first. Why still prioritize it over only practicing retrieval tricks?
check.rubric: correct: Encoding skill takes longer to build but flattens forgetting and eventually eases learning. mostly_correct: Worth it vaguely. incorrect: Encoding is instant; retrieval replaces all encoding.
check.exemplar: Encoding skills take weeks to months to build, longer than retrieval tricks, but they flatten forgetting so I keep more after a strong pass. Eventually learning feels easier. Retrieval alone doesn't replace organizing on the way in.

days.review: Unifying principle: for every new piece, ask what its purpose is and where it fits relative to everything else. The brain keeps what it judges relevant — and relevant means connected. 'It's on the exam' isn't enough.

task.do: Take 5 new or recent facts/ideas from your material. For each, write: purpose (why it exists in the topic) + fit (where it sits relative to the big picture). No orphan one-liners.
task.capture: Five items each with purpose + fit.

check.q: If any of your five items only said 'might be on the test' as purpose, why is that a weak relevance signal for the brain?
check.rubric: correct: Exam threat isn't a connection; relevance = how it fits the big picture. mostly_correct: Need better reasons vaguely. incorrect: Exam reminders fully encode any fact.
check.exemplar: Telling my brain it's on the exam isn't a real connection — it doesn't create relevance. Relevance means purpose and fit relative to the big picture. Without that, the piece stays orphaned even if high-stakes.

check.q: Pick your strongest purpose+fit line. What makes it strong encoding intent compared with a copied definition?
check.rubric: correct: Clear purpose + specific structural link. mostly_correct: Mentions connection vaguely. incorrect: Highlight color or 'important' with no reason.
check.exemplar: A clear purpose plus a specific link to the topic's structure is strong encoding intent. A copied definition with no fit is intake without relevance. 'Important' without a reason doesn't place the piece.

check.q: For an orphan item with no fit, what will you do next — and why isn't memorizing it harder in isolation the fix?
check.rubric: correct: Hold aside until it belongs in the structure; isolation memorizing fails relevance. mostly_correct: Find a place vaguely. incorrect: Memorize harder in isolation; abandon big picture.
check.exemplar: I'll hold it aside until I find where it belongs in the structure. Memorizing orphans harder still leaves them irrelevant to the brain. Encoding requires placing pieces relative to the whole.

days.review: At the moment of learning, simplify ideas until they slot into a simple big picture. Find the simplest concepts and build the simplest whole first — scaffolding. You're not ready for every detail yet; your brain would drop them anyway.

task.do: Open a dense section. Write the simplest 4–7 idea skeleton that captures the whole — no rare details. Park details in a separate 'later' list. Stop when the skeleton is sayable in under a minute.

check.q: Is your skeleton simple enough, or packed with exceptions? What does simplify-first scaffolding require at the moment of learning?
check.rubric: correct: Simplest whole first; park details; not every exception yet. mostly_correct: Keep it simple vaguely. incorrect: More detail always improves first-pass encoding.
check.exemplar: If the skeleton is packed with exceptions, I skipped simplify-first. Scaffolding means the simplest 4–7 ideas that capture the whole, details parked for later. The brain drops excess detail before a stable picture exists.

check.q: Can you say the skeleton in under a minute? What does that (or failure) tell you about whether a simple big picture is forming?
check.rubric: correct: Sayable skeleton = simple big picture forming; unspeakable dump = not simplified. mostly_correct: Mentions clarity vaguely. incorrect: Simple can't be academic; only full detail dumps encode.
check.exemplar: If I can say it in ~45 seconds, a simple big picture is forming. An unspeakable detail dump means I haven't simplified. Simplifying until the whole is graspable is the point of scaffolding.

check.q: How should you use the parked details list across the next sessions — and what order mistake would undo the scaffold?
check.rubric: correct: Add later in layers once skeleton holds; don't memorize parked list first. mostly_correct: Add later vaguely. incorrect: Memorize parked list before any skeleton; throw away skeleton.
check.exemplar: I'll add parked details later in layers once the skeleton holds. Memorizing the parked list before any skeleton undoes scaffolding. Mixing all details back in unordered recreates overwhelm.

days.review: Once the simple skeleton is stable, add one layer of detail, fit it to the big picture, then another. In the study demo, early pages were slow; later pages accelerated because new detail snapped onto a framework.

task.do: Using yesterday's or today's skeleton for a real topic, add exactly one detail layer (a handful of specifics). For each add-on, write how it attaches to the skeleton. Do not add a second layer yet.
task.capture: Skeleton reminder; layer-1 details + attachment notes.

check.q: Do your layer-1 details attach to skeleton nodes? If some don't, what does that say about layered learning?
check.rubric: correct: Unattached details = layering failed; each add-on must fit the big picture. mostly_correct: Need connections vaguely. incorrect: Unattached details encode best.
check.exemplar: Details that don't attach to any skeleton node mean layering failed — I'm collecting orphans again. Each layer must fit the big picture. Unattached specifics aren't a successful layer.

check.q: Why did today's task allow only one detail layer before another — what stabilizes between layers?
check.rubric: correct: Stabilize fit before piling more detail. mostly_correct: Don't rush vaguely. incorrect: Only one fact exists; dump all detail at once for speed.
check.exemplar: I add one layer, see how it fits, then add another — layered learning. Stabilizing fit prevents an unsorted pile. Dumping all detail at once recreates the pre-scaffold mess.

check.q: If adding detail started to feel faster mid-topic, what likely cause matches the encoding demo pattern?
check.rubric: correct: Structure stabilizing — new detail snaps on quicker. mostly_correct: Getting used to it vaguely. incorrect: Speed means abandon skeleton.
check.exemplar: Structure is stabilizing — new detail attaches quicker once the framework holds. That's the demo pattern: early pages slow, later pages accelerate. Speeding up isn't a reason to abandon the skeleton.

days.review: Organize as knowledge arrives — like tidying a room as you go. Dumping everything to reorganize later (or never) is much harder. Practice placing each new idea correctly on entry.

task.do: Study a short new chunk. Rule: every new idea must be placed onto your map/skeleton before you take the next one. No 'inbox dump' list. If placement is unclear, pause and simplify.
task.capture: Chunk studied; placement decisions; any pause-to-simplify moments.

check.q: Did you dump ideas to 'organize tonight,' or place each on entry? How does that choice match organize-on-the-way-in?
check.rubric: correct: Place as knowledge arrives; dumping for later conflicts. mostly_correct: Organize sooner vaguely. incorrect: Dumping first is recommended encoding.
check.exemplar: A long unsorted capture to organize tonight conflicts with organizing on the way in. It's far easier to place knowledge correctly as it arrives than to dump and reorganize later. Tonight-organization rarely equals on-entry placement.

check.q: You may have paused when an idea wouldn't place. Why is that a good instinct for encoding?
check.rubric: correct: Unclear placement → simplify/organize before adding more. mostly_correct: Slow down vaguely. incorrect: Never pause; speed-read past confusion.
check.exemplar: Pausing when placement is unclear is right — unclear means simplify or fix structure before adding more. Speed-reading past confusion keeps dumping orphans. If it doesn't fit, fix the structure.

check.q: What evidence in your capture shows you organized on entry rather than promising to sort later?
check.rubric: correct: Each idea has a decided place now. mostly_correct: Somewhat organized vaguely. incorrect: Messy inbox or vow to reorganize on break week.
check.exemplar: Each idea having a decided place in the structure now is evidence of on-entry organization. A messy inbox or a vow to reorganize during break week is a dump. Highlights with no placement aren't organized.

days.review: Don't study for weeks then test once. Effective learning loops hypothesis → feedback → refine. As each piece arrives, guess how it connects, then check. Wrong guesses early are cheap; wrong assumptions carried for weeks are expensive. Lightbulb moments are confirmed hypotheses.

task.do: For 3 incoming ideas in your material: before checking the source's framing, write a quick hypothesis of how each connects. Then check and mark confirm / adjust / reject. Refine one connection that was wrong.

check.q: Some hypotheses may have been wrong but caught quickly. What does that teach about iteration and the cost of early errors?
check.rubric: correct: Early wrong guesses are cheap; loop is the point. mostly_correct: Mistakes OK vaguely. incorrect: Wrong guesses mean stop hypothesizing.
check.exemplar: Wrong hypotheses caught in minutes show early errors are cheap — iteration working. The loop is guess → check → refine. Waiting weeks to test makes wrong assumptions expensive.

check.q: If you avoided guessing to 'not be wrong,' what cost does that create for encoding?
check.rubric: correct: Delays feedback; may carry silent wrong assumptions longer. mostly_correct: Less learning vaguely. incorrect: Avoiding hypotheses maximizes insight.
check.exemplar: Avoiding guesses delays feedback and may let silent wrong assumptions ride for weeks. Iteration needs testable hypotheses. Being wrong once in a micro-loop doesn't ruin encoding — hiding from error does.

check.q: After a rejected hypothesis, what micro-loop will you run next?
check.rubric: correct: Revised connection → re-check quickly. mostly_correct: Try again vaguely. incorrect: Wait weeks; memorize wrong version; stop relating.
check.exemplar: I'll write a revised connection and re-check quickly — hypothesis → feedback → refine. Waiting weeks before any test loses the iteration effect. Memorizing the wrong version harder makes it worse.

days.review: Practical iteration: right after learning a chunk, look away and try to reproduce or use it immediately. If you can't, encoding (or struggle level) needs work — and you just got instant feedback. Test to the max in tiny loops.

task.do: Learn one small chunk from your material (3–5 minutes). Close it. Reproduce the structure/use from memory for 2 minutes. Open, note gaps, fix encoding (relink/simplify), then micro-retrieve once more.
task.capture: First reproduction; gaps; fix; second reproduction result.

check.q: Your first micro-retrieval may have failed. How should you interpret that signal for encoding quality right now?
check.rubric: correct: Useful feedback — encoding or struggle needs work now; cheap to fix. mostly_correct: Need to restudy vaguely. incorrect: Never retrieve early; only end-of-month tests matter.
check.exemplar: A bad first reproduction is useful signal — encoding or struggle needs work now, while fixes are cheap. It doesn't mean abandon the topic or wait for a monthly test. Immediate failure is feedback on how ideas went in.

check.q: After you fixed links and tried again, what did the second retrieval tell you about the iteration loop?
check.rubric: correct: Improvement confirms fix; hypothesis/fix/refine in action. mostly_correct: Got better vaguely. incorrect: Skip second retrieval; retrieval harms encoding.
check.exemplar: If the second retrieval improved after relinking/simplifying, the iteration loop worked — form, refine, test again. Micro-retrieval confirms whether encoding improved. Skipping the second try leaves the fix unverified.

check.q: What micro-retrieval prompt will you use right after the next chunk — and why not reread and assume mastery?
check.rubric: correct: Look away and rebuild/use without peeking. mostly_correct: Self-test vaguely. incorrect: Reread once; highlight; watch summary instead of producing.
check.exemplar: I'll look away and rebuild or use the chunk without peeking — test to the max. Rereading and assuming mastery skips the feedback. Producing immediately after learning is the practical iteration move.

days.review: First laying out a big topic feels overwhelming. That discomfort is cognitive load doing its job — confusion as fuel. Work through it by simplifying and organizing, not by writing more undigested notes.

task.do: Choose a topic that currently feels confusing. For 8 minutes, only simplify and organize (skeleton + placements). Ban adding new copied notes. End by rating confusion 1–10 before vs after.
task.capture: Before/after confusion ratings; simplified structure; what you refused to copy.

check.q: When confusion was high, did you start copying more paragraphs? How does that conflict with using confusion as fuel?
check.rubric: correct: Fix is simplify/organize, not write more undigested notes. mostly_correct: Organize instead vaguely. incorrect: More copying is the cure; stop structuring.
check.exemplar: Copying more paragraphs conflicts with the lesson — writing more isn't the fix. Confusion is cognitive load to channel by simplifying and organizing. Overwhelm doesn't prove encoding is impossible.

check.q: If your confusion rating dropped after scaffolding, how do you read that change?
check.rubric: correct: Load channeled into useful structure. mostly_correct: Felt clearer vaguely. incorrect: Drop means cheated; confusion should never decrease.
check.exemplar: A drop after scaffolding means cognitive load was channeled into useful structure. Confusion as fuel worked. The rating change tracks encoding progress when the response is simplify/organize.

check.q: A new map looks messy at first. What mindset keeps you encoding instead of quitting or dumping more detail?
check.rubric: correct: Expected; stay with simplify/organize until stable. mostly_correct: Keep going vaguely. incorrect: Quit higher-order encoding; dump more detail to hide mess.
check.exemplar: Messy first layouts are expected — I'll stay with simplify/organize until it stabilizes. Quitting or dumping more undigested detail hides the mess without encoding. Overwhelm at first big-picture work is normal.

days.review: Encoding is mostly how you think, not which fancy tool you use. Pull it together on one real topic: relate, simplify, layer once, organize on entry, micro-retrieve.

task.do: One topic, ~10 minutes: build a simple big picture, place 5–8 ideas with purpose/fit, add one detail layer, then closed-book reproduce the skeleton. No passive-only reread.
task.capture: Big picture; placements; layer-1 adds; reproduction result.

check.q: Beautiful notes with a failed closed-book skeleton — what does that say about tools/output versus encoding?
check.rubric: correct: Pretty output ≠ encoding; reproduction still weak. mostly_correct: Need recall vaguely. incorrect: Pretty notes guarantee flattened forgetting.
check.exemplar: Failed skeleton recall means tool/output isn't encoding — the thinking and reproduction are still weak. You can encode well from a plain book by relating and simplifying. Pretty notes don't flatten forgetting by themselves.

check.q: Which part of your capture best shows real encoding rather than busywork — and why?
check.rubric: correct: Purpose/fit placements + successful skeleton retrieval. mostly_correct: Mentions structure vaguely. incorrect: Word count, colors, or hours without recall.
check.exemplar: Purpose/fit placements plus a successful skeleton retrieval show encoding. Word count, pastel colors, or hours without checking recall are busywork. Connected placement plus immediate reproduce is the loop.

check.q: If layer-1 details wouldn't attach, what will you do before forcing more detail — and why not isolate them on flashcards only?
check.rubric: correct: Simplify skeleton until attachments clear; then retry. mostly_correct: Fix structure vaguely. incorrect: Force isolated flashcards; abandon big picture.
check.exemplar: I'll simplify the skeleton until attachments are clear, then retry the layer. Forcing unattached details onto isolated flashcards abandons the big picture. Unattached detail means the scaffold needs work first.

days.review: Checkpoint: big-picture fit, simplify-first, on-entry organization, and micro-retrieval — fresh scenarios on your own material.

task.do: New dense page/section: (1) 60-second simplified skeleton, (2) place 4 ideas with fit, (3) one hypothesis-check on a connection, (4) immediate closed-book reproduce.
task.capture: Skeleton; four fits; hypothesis outcome; reproduce result.

check.q: If you jumped to memorizing details before any skeleton, what encoding rule did you violate — and what order will you use instead?
check.rubric: correct: Violates simplify-first; simplest whole then layers. mostly_correct: Big picture first vaguely. incorrect: Details always precede big picture.
check.exemplar: That violates simplify-first scaffolding. I'll build a 60-second simple skeleton first, then place ideas, then layer details. Details before relevance recreates orphans.

check.q: Walk through your hypothesis outcome and reproduce result. How does that pattern show healthy (or unhealthy) iteration?
check.rubric: correct: Wrong→caught→refine→improved reproduce = healthy cheap error loop. mostly_correct: Learned from mistake vaguely. incorrect: Wrong hypotheses forbid further encoding; wait weeks to reproduce.
check.exemplar: Hypothesis wrong, caught same session, then reproduce improved — healthy iteration: cheap error, fast refine, test again. Only perfect first guesses aren't required. Waiting weeks to reproduce makes errors expensive.

check.q: Fresh overwhelm mid-map: what response treats confusion as fuel, and what responses make encoding worse?
check.rubric: correct: Simplify/organize; don't copy more, only highlight, or quit structuring. mostly_correct: Calm down by organizing vaguely. incorrect: Longer undigested notes until calm.
check.exemplar: I'll simplify and organize — confusion as fuel. Adding longer undigested notes, only highlighting, or quitting structure makes encoding worse. Hard subjects still need big-picture placement.
